lesson.title: The Twin Suppletions
lesson.subtitle: bon → meilleur (ameliorate) and mauvais → pire (pejorative): frozen Latin comparatives.

hook.title: Why 'Good → Better' and 'Bon → Meilleur' Are Historical Twins
hook.content: bon ('good') jumps to meilleur ('better', cousin of 'ameliorate'), and mauvais ('bad') jumps to pire ('worse', cousin of 'pejorative')! And putting le, la, or les in front of any comparative turns it into the superlative: le meilleur ('the best'), le plus grand ('the biggest')!

footnotes.title: Putting le / la / les in front makes the Superlative ('the best / the biggest')!
footnotes.content: plus grand que = 'bigger than'; le plus grand = 'the biggest'. meilleur que = 'better than'; le meilleur / la meilleure = 'the best'!

pattern.title: Comparative + le/la/les in Front = Superlative ('the -est')
pattern.content: Use meilleur/pire for better/worse and prefix le/la/les for the best/worst.
pattern.linguist_note: Romance analytic superlatives are formed by prefixing the definite article to the comparative degree.
pattern.trap_note: Never say *le plus bon for 'the best' — 'better' is meilleur, and 'the best' is le meilleur / la meilleure!

exercises.prompt: Match each comparative or superlative form with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: le plus grand / la plus grande

exercises.target_answer: better than, the best, worse than, bigger than, the biggest
exercises.meaning: meilleur que (never *plus bon), le meilleur / la meilleure, pire que (pejorative), plus grand que, le plus grand / la plus grande
exercises.explanation: Putting le/la/les in front of any comparative turns '-er' into 'the -est'!

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'It is the best restaurant in the city'?
options: C'est le plus bon restaurant dans la ville
C'est meilleur restaurant de la ville
C'est le meilleur restaurant de la ville
exercises.target_answer: C'est le meilleur restaurant de la ville
exercises.meaning: It is the best restaurant in the city
exercises.explanation: le meilleur = 'the best', and after a superlative French uses de ('of the city')!

exercises.prompt: Turn 'meilleure' ('better', f.) into the feminine superlative 'the best':

exercises.idea: this bakery has the best bread (use Cette boulangerie a le meilleur pain)
cues: This bakery has → Cette boulangerie a
the best bread → le meilleur pain
exercises.target_answer: Cette boulangerie a le meilleur pain
exercises.meaning: This bakery has the best bread

diagnosis.cue: Use le meilleur pain for 'the best bread'.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Ce café est meilleur que l'autre
exercises.target_answer: Ce café est meilleur que l'autre
exercises.meaning: This coffee is better than the other one
exercises.affirmation: You paired meilleur with que l'autre cleanly.

summary.outcome: Use irregular comparatives meilleur ('better') and pire ('worse'), and form superlatives by adding le/la/les.

use_example.german: C'est la meilleure idée de la journée.
use_example.english: It's the best idea of the day.

summary.takeaway: Add le/la/les to any comparative to make the superlative: meilleur → le meilleur ('the best').
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2102] Comparison Gym): see how The Twin Suppletions leads directly into Comparison Gym.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "This bakery has the best bread" in French:
twist.target_answer: Cette boulangerie a le meilleur pain
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Cette boulangerie a le meilleur pain" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Twin Suppletions.

meilleur.etymology_derivation: Latin melior — English 'ameliorate'. bon→meilleur is good→better's twin suppletion: both languages froze an old comparative.

bon.etymology_derivation: Latin bonus 'good' — English borrowed the word back as 'bonus', a good thing added.

plus.etymology_derivation: borrowed into English whole — plus is plus. The final s falls silent in most positions.

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

vin.context_translation: I would like some red wine.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.

gâteau.etymology_derivation: Old French gastel, from Frankish *wastil. English 'gateau' narrowed to a rich cake; French kept the everyday word — form travels, meaning drifts.
